plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 9: Systems of Equations and Inequalities
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows three mutually perpendicular planes cutting through one another, drawn as flat colored parallelograms with no coordinate axes displayed. A green plane stands roughly upright facing the viewer, labeled x = 1 in matching green at its upper right. A red plane meets it at a right angle, tilted so it reads as a tall diamond passing behind and around the green sheet, labeled y = -2 in red beneath the drawing. A blue plane lies nearly horizontal and slices through both others, labeled z = 2 in blue at its right edge. The sheets overlap so each is partly hidden by the others, giving a sectioned, interlocking block in which the visible pieces alternate in color where they cross. A small black dot near the center is labeled (1, -1, 2), which conflicts with the red plane label y = -2; as drawn, the displayed point does not satisfy all three displayed plane equations. The drawing still gives geometric meaning to a system of three linear equations in three variables, but the plane label or point label must be corrected before the marked point can be treated as the simultaneous solution.

elements: green vertical plane x = 1, drawn as an upright parallelogram facing the viewer
red plane y = -2 (as printed), drawn as a tall diamond tilted perpendicular to the green plane
blue near-horizontal plane z = 2, slicing through both other planes
small black dot marking the point near the common intersection
leader line from the dot to the label '(1, -1, 2)'
green label 'x = 1' at the upper right of the green plane
red label 'y = -2' beneath the drawing
blue label 'z = 2' at the right edge of the blue plane
warning badge (appears when a plane the point fails to satisfy is shown): the point does not lie on y = -2

interactions.label: x = 1 (green)
interactions.teaches: A single equation in 3 variables pins only one coordinate: the green sheet holds every point whose x-coordinate is 1, no matter what y and z are

interactions.label: y = -2 (red)
interactions.teaches: Turning on the red plane shows that the labeled point (1, -1, 2) is NOT on it — a warning highlights that y = -1 fails the equation y = -2, so the printed figure is inconsistent

interactions.label: z = 2 (blue)
interactions.teaches: The blue sheet holds every point at height z = 2; only the line where it cuts a vertical plane belongs to both
Clicking a colored equation highlights its plane and names the one coordinate it fixes, showing that each equation removes one degree of freedom but leaves a whole sheet of candidates

interactions.label: Figure version
interactions.teaches: A solution of a 3x3 system must satisfy every equation at once: sliding the red plane from y = -2 to y = -1 makes all three planes pass through the dot, so (1, -1, 2) becomes the unique simultaneous solution

demo_steps.title: The printed figure
demo_steps.narration: All three planes are shown. The dot at (1, -1, 2) sits on the green and blue planes, but the warning shows it misses the red plane y = -2 — the printed figure cannot be a solution picture as labeled.

demo_steps.title: One plane at a time
demo_steps.narration: Hide the red and blue planes. The green plane x = 1 alone contains infinitely many points — one equation leaves a full sheet of candidates, not a single point.

demo_steps.title: The corrected system
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the corrected version: the red plane slides to y = -1 and now passes through the dot. All three planes meet in exactly one point, (1, -1, 2) — the unique solution of the system.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a small world: planes ~4 x 4 world-unit square sheets centered near the origin, rendered as double-sided semi-transparent (opacity ~0.85) MeshPhongMaterial so the interlocking overlap reads like the source. Map world coordinates directly to the point: dot at (1, yPlane, 2) with scale 1 unit per coordinate, so with the corrected y = -1 the dot sits at (1, -1, 2) and all three planes pass through it. Green plane x = 1: the plane x = 1, upright, facing the viewer, green #2e9e4f, label 'x = 1' at its upper right in matching green. Red plane: the plane y = c where c is -2 (as printed) or -1 (corrected); tall diamond reading as perpendicular to the green sheet, red #d43a2f, label 'y = -2'/'y = -1' below the drawing in red; animate the red plane sliding between y = -2 and y = -1 on version switch. Blue plane z = 2: near-horizontal, blue #1f77b4, label 'z = 2' at its right edge in blue. Dot: black sphere radius ~0.08 at (1, -1, 2) with a thin leader line to the label '(1, -1, 2)' above-right. In the as-printed version the dot is visibly OFF the red plane (offset by 1 unit along y) — keep this offset visible; the warning badge appears over/near the red label whenever the red plane is visible in the as-printed version. Camera: axonometric three-quarter view matching the source (green sheet roughly frontal, blue sheet receding).
interactionPlan.notes: Three.js: render planes with DoubleSide and depthWrite true; slight polygonOffset per plane to avoid z-fighting at intersection lines. Optionally draw the pairwise intersection lines (thin darker lines) where planes cross to emphasize that two equations give a line and three give a point. The correction toggle lerps the red plane's y-position between -2 and -1 and swaps the red label text; the dot and its label never move. Warning badge: HTML overlay or sprite shown only in as-printed mode with showY true. Click interaction: raycast against planes and label sprites; highlight by raising emissive intensity and displaying 'fixes x = 1' (etc.) text.
